title: The Teenager Whose Anemia Had No Name — A Lifetime of Infections, Jaundice, and an Unresolved Diagnosis

sections.heading: The Patient's Story
sections.content:
She is 15 years old, the first child of a consanguineous marriage. Her mother died during the birth of her third child. She has two younger brothers, both apparently healthy.

Her story goes back to early childhood. Since she was very young, she has had recurrent respiratory infections — colds, fevers, and productive coughs — that worsened every winter. For the past four years, she has had intermittent yellowing of her eyes, not linked to fever, without itching, and without signs suggestive of chronic liver disease. Alongside this, she has had easy fatigability, generalized weakness, and loss of appetite for four years, which became markedly worse in the last two to three months. She is short for her age, has struggled to gain weight appropriately, and had delayed development of secondary sexual characteristics. She reached menarche in October 2020 and has now had two months of amenorrhea.

Looking back at her records, her illness has been a long, tangled thread. At age 2 (2005), weighing just 7.3 kg, she first presented with fever and cough; a chest X-ray showed a consolidation, and she was treated empirically for tuberculosis for two months, though her symptoms persisted. Over the following years she was seen again and again for recurrent lower respiratory tract infections, ear infections, and fevers — repeatedly treated with antibiotics and, on at least two separate occasions (ages 3 and roughly a year later), given further courses of anti-tubercular therapy based on positive Mantoux tests, without lasting resolution of her symptoms. At age 8, imaging showed prominent bronchi and ground-glass opacities in her lungs, along with borderline splenomegaly. Between ages 9 and 14, she continued to have repeated respiratory infections, growing only slowly (13 kg at age 9, 16 kg at age 11), and was worked up for failure to thrive and protein-energy malnutrition, with several possible explanations considered at the time (tuberculosis, bronchiolitis, enteric fever, reactive airway disease) without a definitive answer.

In 2016, at around age 12, she developed jaundice for the first time — hemoglobin 9.0, mildly elevated bilirubin — treated as possible viral hepatitis and requiring one blood transfusion; her jaundice then resolved and did not return for three years. Recurrent lung infections and chest X-ray abnormalities (including an interlobar effusion and bilateral upper lobe consolidations) continued through 2016 and 2017.

In late 2017, she was evaluated for a possible congenital heart defect (a moderate ventricular septal defect was seen on one echocardiogram but not confirmed on a repeat study elsewhere) and was followed for two years for presumed allergic bronchitis, tried on multiple inhalers and medications for her recurrent lung infections without improvement. Growth hormone testing in 2019 was normal, though ultrasound around that time showed moderate splenomegaly and her hemoglobin had dropped to 8.1.

In mid-2020, she developed loss of appetite and intermittent abdominal pain. Her jaundice recurred in October 2020, resolved on its own, then returned again in January 2021 and this time did not go away — accompanied by mild splenomegaly on ultrasound, prompting consideration of Gilbert syndrome or a hemolytic process. An upper GI endoscopy was normal. By late January 2021, her hemoglobin had fallen sharply to 5.6, with a markedly abnormal blood count showing macrocytic, normochromic cells with teardrop forms and ovalocytes; hemoglobin electrophoresis was essentially normal, and urine testing was positive for bile salts and pigments.

She was admitted to a tertiary center under gastroenterology for over a week, where her anemia workup (reticulocyte count, kidney function, direct and indirect Coombs tests, thyroid function, celiac and autoimmune markers, G6PD level) was largely unremarkable apart from a raised LDH. She was sent home on oral iron and B12.

Four days later, her weakness, appetite loss, and jaundice worsened sharply, and she was admitted to a local hospital where she received two more blood transfusions. Her hemoglobin improved temporarily with transfusion but fell again afterward. She was then taken to another government hospital and subsequently to a corporate hospital, where autoimmune hemolytic anemia was suspected; clinical exome sequencing was sent (result pending) and she was started on oral steroids (prednisolone) at the start of March 2021. Despite this, her jaundice and weakness suddenly worsened again, prompting her family to bring her to this hospital.

sections.heading: What the Work-Up Showed So Far
sections.content:
**On this admission:**

- **General appearance:** short, thin build, weight 28 kg; marked pallor and icterus; no lymphadenopathy or pedal edema; raised JVP
- **Respiratory exam:** reduced chest expansion (more on the right), dull percussion note over the right infrascapular area with reduced air entry there, otherwise resonant
- **Abdominal exam:** normal shape, central inverted umbilicus, non-tender, no local warmth; mild splenomegaly, no hepatomegaly; bowel sounds present, no free fluid
- **Blood counts:** hemoglobin critically low at 3.2 g/dL, with red cell count 0.8 million, macrocytic indices (MCV 116), and a markedly raised RDW of 25
- **Liver and metabolic panel:** total bilirubin 8.16 mg/dL (mostly indirect), transaminases and alkaline phosphatase near normal, low-normal total protein and albumin with a narrow gamma gap
- **Peripheral smear:** macrocytes, macro-ovalocytes, anisopoikilocytosis with hypochromia
- **Coombs testing:** direct Coombs strongly positive (4+), indirect Coombs weakly positive (1+), and a positive auto-control, indicating an autoimmune hemolytic process; thermal amplitude testing was pending

**Working impressions at this stage** included autoimmune hemolytic anemia, possible common variable immunodeficiency syndrome (given her lifelong pattern of recurrent infections), recurrent respiratory tract infections, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, and failure to thrive.

sections.heading: How the Story Unfolded
sections.content:
The case record also includes a structured summary of her presentation, framed as a 17-year-old (reflecting a later point in her course) presenting with two days of jaundice, exertional breathlessness, fatigue, and pedal edema, against the same lifelong background of recurrent childhood infections, chronic anemia, short stature, growth delay, and delayed menarche.

On this presentation, her vitals showed a fast heart rate (150 bpm), blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and normal blood glucose. Examination revealed severe conjunctival pallor, lemon-yellow scleral icterus, a pale, smooth ("bald") tongue, and no palpable lymph nodes. Her nails showed visible capillary pulsations (Quincke's sign), and she had a venous hum in the neck and visible abdominal aortic pulsations — signs suggesting a high-output circulatory state. She had pitting edema up to both ankles.

On cardiac exam, her precordium was hyperdynamic, with a palpable pulmonic component (P2), a raised JVP, a loud P2 on auscultation, a pansystolic murmur along the left sternal border that increased with inspiration, and an S3 gallop that also increased with inspiration. Occluding forward flow in the right femoral artery while listening revealed a diastolic bruit — another sign consistent with a high-output state. Breath sounds were reduced in intensity. Her abdominal exam now showed moderate splenomegaly and mild hepatomegaly.

Taking her entire history and this examination together, she was diagnosed with autoimmune hemolytic anemia complicated by acute high-output heart failure — her years of unexplained recurrent infections, chronic hemolysis, growth failure, and delayed puberty converging, in this telling, on a single severe and rapidly decompensating illness whose root immunological or genetic cause (the exome sequencing result) remained pending.
